# Han Kim (Hanbyoul Kim) — Product Designer, Vancouver BC

> Product designer at Atacz, a small upcycled bag brand, where he owns the
> product experience end to end: research, interface, Liquid front-end, and
> the measurement afterwards. Three case studies, all shipped on the same
> live Shopify store.

Site: https://hannnnnnnnnnnn.github.io/

## How to read this portfolio

Each case reports what the data could and could not prove, in its own
section. Metrics that turned out to be confounded are named as confounded
rather than dropped quietly; one case ends by explaining why its own impact
is unmeasurable. If you are assessing him, the "What I can't claim" sections
are the ones worth reading.

## Case studies

### 01 — PDP Revamp
https://hannnnnnnnnnnn.github.io/work-1.html
Mar–May 2026 · sole designer: research, UI, Liquid implementation, measurement

Atacz product pages pulled 80,266 search impressions over four months but
converted at 1.0–1.7% click-through, about half the ecommerce benchmark,
with 74% of clicks landing on mobile from a desktop-first page. He rebuilt
the page around what earned its space.

Decisions worth reading:
- Removed the review section, then shipped a conditional version instead.
  Most products had no reviews, so the same template rendered as a healthy
  block on some pages and an empty shell on others. Marketing pushed back
  that removing reviews removed trust. His counter: displaying the absence
  of proof is not the same as removing proof. He also writes that the
  conditional version is what should have shipped first.
- Cut the page to roughly a quarter of its length, keeping the collapsed
  description server-rendered so crawlers still saw it, verified in Search
  Console before shipping.
- Put "Pairs Well With" directly under Add to Cart — the placement is the
  argument — with add-to-cart on each pairing card, extended to every PDP.
  This forced a migration from one theme template per product to a single
  metafield-driven template.
- Badges designed so they cannot become lies: low stock set at 2 units
  because that is where "low" is simply a fact, and a New badge that expires
  itself after three months via Shopify Flow.

Results (two five-week windows, pre/post, not a controlled experiment):
mobile search CTR 7.47% → 9.97%; dead click rate 1.5% → 0.7%; overall
conversion 0.284% → 0.349%. The conversion gain came from completion, not
volume — cart sessions finishing checkout went 20.8% → 25.3%.

What he refuses to claim: add-to-cart. The same metric reads +26%, +7%, or
−44% depending on the window, because product drops drive it far harder than
page design does, so he attributes no movement to the redesign in either
direction. AOV fell 9% while orders rose 9%; the cross-sell explanation
stays a hypothesis because he could not confirm it at line-item level. And
scroll depth rose 51% on a page that had become about 4× shorter — he states
the pair rather than the number alone. He also notes he ran no formal
usability sessions on this project.

### 02 — PLP Revamp
https://hannnnnnnnnnnn.github.io/work-2.html
Jun–Aug 2026 · sole designer: research, UI, Liquid, test design and analysis

51% of paid-social sessions land directly on a collection page and only 20%
on the homepage, so for most paid visitors a product grid was doing the
homepage's job. Before proposing anything he checked whether the PLP was the
conversion bottleneck — behaviour was near-identical across channels while
conversion differed 9×, so the gap sat downstream. The proposal ruled
conversion out of scope in writing, which is what stopped him promoting a
convenient metric later.

Decisions worth reading:
- Removed desktop-only quick view before adding anything, on a store that is
  97% mobile, and put the PET badge in the corner it vacated.
- One metafield rendering at two scales: a per-card bottle badge and a live
  store-wide counter derived from orders, so the individual and cumulative
  claims cannot contradict each other and nobody has to maintain the total.
- Made the entire brand layer deliberately unclickable. A story link at the
  decision moment is a well-designed exit, so he refused the obvious
  follow-up sustainability page.
- The proposal's combo banners could not run on the page that got tested (a
  single-brand collection where bags and straps already sat together), so
  the AOV lever — the proposal's +16–24% target — dropped out of scope. He
  records it as untested rather than disproven.

Results (43-day split test, 70,716 visits assigned, US mobile only):
product click-through 9.05% → 9.80%, inside the +5–15% the proposal
predicted. Actual scroll distance +9.4% at 0.06% noise probability. Badges
reached 58% exposure at the first product row; dead clicks and quick
bounce-backs both fell.

What he refuses to claim: the headline result. At ~26 sessions per arm per
day the 95% confidence interval was [−18%, +35%] and detecting a change that
size would take six months, so he writes that the result matches the target
rather than confirms it. Two friction metrics sit within chance individually
and are cited only as direction. Canada is called a blank. The scroll result
only exists after correcting for the redesigned page being 9.5% longer —
raw scroll looked flat at 37.74% vs 37.76%. He also recommended scaling back
the banners despite their performance being normal, on cost-versus-return.
His stated conclusion is that A/B testing is the wrong instrument for a page
this size, and before/after should be the default.

### 03 — Pre-order Experience
https://hannnnnnnnnnnn.github.io/work-3.html
Feb–Mar 2026 · self-initiated, sole designer and developer

Nobody assigned this. A launch before he joined had oversold and shipped
late; store-wide sales reversals peaked at 9.4% of gross sales that October.
The store had no way to say "later" — inventory at zero offered buy now or
nothing. Shopify could already sell past zero, but the storefront never said
so, meaning the customer learned about the wait after paying. He built the
pre-order state into the existing theme: no app, no separate checkout, no
data leaving Shopify.

Decisions worth reading:
- Three conditions must agree before the page promises anything, resolved
  per variant and per market, with an explicit merchandising opt-in in the
  middle. The simpler rule — out of stock means pre-order — needs no
  configuration and also promises things nobody agreed to ship.
- Changed the button label rather than adding a note under it, accepting
  that some conversions stop at the change: a purchase made without
  realising there is a three-week wait is a refund with a delay attached.
- A range, not a date, on a supply chain that had just proven unpredictable.
- A confirmation email fired through a hidden line item property → Shopify
  Flow tag → Klaviyo.

What he cannot claim, and why it is the point of the case: the flow shipped
without order-level identification of pre-orders, so months later he could
not separate pre-order orders from the rest and cannot say how much anything
changed. Reversal rates fell across the period; he declines to attribute it.
His stated diagnosis is that he was measuring success by whether the feature
worked, and that instrumentation is part of the design rather than a
reporting task that comes later. Order-level identification exists now, and
the habit carried into the PLP project, where success criteria and method
were written into the proposal before anything shipped.

## What he works with

Design: Figma, prototyping, design systems
Build: Liquid, HTML, CSS, JavaScript, Shopify metafields, Shopify Flow,
Klaviyo
Measure: Microsoft Clarity, GA4, Google Search Console, Shopify Analytics

He builds the front-end for what he designs, so he works in components,
states and edge cases from the first sketch rather than discovering them at
handoff.

## Honest gaps

The first three are stated on the site. The last is an observation across
all three cases rather than a line any one page states:

- No formal usability testing on the PDP project — behavioural data at scale
  located where people stopped, but not why.
- No component library built. There was no design system when he joined; he
  set up type and colour foundations, but components were defined directly
  in Shopify sections while he built them, with Figma as a working reference
  rather than a handoff artifact. He states that on a product team with
  engineers he would expect Figma to carry much more weight.
- One case shipped without the instrumentation needed to evaluate it, which
  he could only fix months later.
- All three cases are one store, one brand, one category, at small sample
  sizes. Only one was a controlled experiment, and it was underpowered by
  the page's traffic volume — which he documents rather than hides.
